newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong democrats flay "contemptible" US, UK.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong democrats flay "contemptible" US, UK.

text.p: Hong Kong democrats, fearful for their future under communist Chinese rule, on Thursday bitterly charged the United States and Britain with betrayal for easing their stand against a Beijing-picked legislature.

Political analysts described the decision by the two countries to send their top Hong Kong envoys to the swearing-in of new lawmakers after the handover from Britain as a pragmatic move to protect their business interests in booming China.
But Emily Lau, an outspoken champion of democracy, condemned London and Washington as "disgusting and contemptible".

"I am not surprised," she said of the decision, which severely blunts the impact of a boycott of the ceremony by visiting U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and British Prime Minister Tony Blair.
Democratic Party leader Martin Lee said the original message that Britain and China would not accept the legitimacy of the new chamber "is much watered-down, if not contradicted".
The provisional legislature, which will be sworn in shortly after the midnight Monday handover ceremony, replaces a democratically-elected body. Both Lee and Lau will be excluded.

Underlining the commercial realities that lay behind the U-turn, Hong Kong stocks on Thursday ignored the political row and continued their surge on "handover fever". The biggest gainers were "red chip" companies backed by Beijing.
Britain and the United States have huge investments in Hong Kong, a gateway to trade with China.

Behind the political trauma, preparations went ahead for an end-of-empire party, a Hollywood-style extravaganza that will light up the skies over Hong Kong with fireworks and fill the air with the sounds of symphony orchestras, dragon-dance drums, military bands and mass karaoke.

Fireworks barges were towed into place, and police frogmen scoured the harbour for bombs in preparation for the arrival of dozens of dignitaries, including Chinese President Jiang Zemin and Britain's heir-to-the-throne Prince Charles.

British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook planned to tell the European Union in Luxembourg on Thursday why British ministers would boycott the swearing-in, but officials said he would not plead with the EU to follow suit.
British media reports said Cook would urge his partners to follow Britain's lead but a senior official said this approach would be too risky.
"I don't think it would help the people of Hong Kong to run a high-profile campaign which didn't work," said the official, who asked not to be identified.
Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten, who infuriated Beijing by broadening democracy in the waning years of Britain's colonial rule, defended his one-man-one-vote crusade.
"Pluralism is the sound of the future in Asia and everywhere else," he said in an interview with the British newspaper, The Independent.
Washington decided to send Hong Kong Consul General Richard Boucher and London its two top Hong Kong diplomats, Francis Cornish and Hugh Davies, to the legislature swearing-in.
Political analysts said the flip-flop left Britain's boycott policy in tatters and Patten's tough pro-democracy campaign against China in shreds.
"Britain is belly up," said an analyst close to the government. "It's almost a kowtow."
"We're witnessing the end of British confrontation with China," analyst Sonny Lo at Hong Kong University's politics department.

An editorial in the South China Morning Post, the territory's main English-language newspaper, said Britain and the United States had lost the moral high ground. It accused them of "shilly-shallying edging towards hypocrisy".
A cartoon in The Hong Kong Standard depicted the United States, Britain and big business trooping into the swearing-in with Lee outside crying: "They're selling us out."
As the swearing-in ceremony gets under way, Lee and his supporters have said they will peacefully invade the colonial-style legislature building and denounce the new assembly from an outside balcony.
Opinion polls released on Thursday indicated the new legislature lacked significant public support.
